question.prompt: The numbers \(1,\) \(2,\) \(\ldots,\) \(9\) are randomly placed into the \(9\) squares of a \(3 \times 3\) grid. Each square gets one number, and each of the numbers is used once. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers in each row and each column is odd?

solutions.title: Count the odd-number patterns
solutions.explanation:
Only parity matters. A row or column has an odd sum exactly when it contains one or three odd numbers.

There are five odd numbers altogether. Therefore, if every row has odd sum, the numbers of odd entries in the three rows must be \(3,1,1\), in some order. The same reasoning applies to the columns. Thus there is exactly one all-odd row and exactly one all-odd column.

Their union contains \(3+3-1=5\) squares, so these are precisely the five odd-number positions. Conversely, any such row-and-column pattern gives every row and column either one or three odd entries, as required.

There are \(3\cdot3=9\) valid patterns. None is counted twice, since its all-odd row and column are unique. Altogether, the four even-number positions can be chosen in \(\binom94=126\) ways. These patterns are equally likely because each allows exactly \(4!5!\) arrangements of the actual numbers.

Hence the probability is
\[
\frac{9}{126}=\boxed{\frac1{14}},
\]
which is choice \(\text{B}\).
